strengths: A highly novel application of reinforcement learning (GRPO) to explicitly optimize the efficiency-accuracy trade-off of MLLMs, transitioning from exploiting passive/emergent sparsity to active reinforcement of token sparsity.

Extremely thorough and comprehensive evaluation across 13 diverse benchmarks (covering both image and video modalities) and multiple state-of-the-art MLLM backbones (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-Video).

Impressive empirical results showing that Sparsity Forcing achieves a ~75% reduction in visual tokens (retaining only ~24% of tokens) with negligible performance degradation compared to the dense model baselines.
Insightful analysis and visualizations, such as showing the layer-wise token retention before/after training, scaling behavior with long context lengths, and sensitivity on HallusionBench.
weaknesses: Training efficiency is a major bottleneck. As the authors point out in the limitations, executing sequential rollouts for different budgets (due to different dynamic attention masks and KV-caches) prevents standard batching and makes RL training slow.

Lack of clarity on how answer correctness ($r_{\text{per}}$) is programmatically evaluated during RL training (e.g., whether it uses exact match, parser rules, or an LLM-as-a-judge), which is critical for reproducibility.

It is unclear if fine-tuning the model for visual token sparsity compromises its performance on other capabilities (e.g., pure text-only benchmarks, general safety, or conversational abilities), as no text-only evaluation is reported.

strengths: Novel and well-designed RL framework: Proposes Sparsity Forcing, which utilizes Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize both MLLM performance and token sparsity. This avoids proxy objectives (like attention sharpness regularizers) and directly aligns the model for inference-time efficiency.

Robust Reward Design: The introduction of the group-level indicator $C$ is a clever and effective way to prevent the 'efficiency-bias' collapse during training, ensuring that token reduction is only encouraged when accuracy is maintained.

Thorough and extensive evaluation: Tested on 13 popular benchmarks across both image and video modalities. The results show consistent capability to reduce token retention to ~24% with negligible performance drop, outperforming existing post-training or training-free baselines like FastV, ZipVL, MOBA, and sharpness loss.

Impressive real-world speedups: Provides real wall-clock latency (up to 3.3x) and memory savings (up to 3.0x) on long context sequences (up to 200k), which is highly relevant for deploying long-context video models.
weaknesses: Training overhead and batching constraints: As admitted in the limitations, the multi-budget rollout scheme requires executing rollouts sequentially because each budget (threshold p) creates a different sparse mask and KV-cache. This significantly increases training time and prevents efficient parallel batching during the RL phase.

KL Divergence Mismatch Clarification: In the objective function (Eq 11), the policy model $\pi_\theta$ (which uses sparse attention, specifically ZipVL) is regularized using KL divergence against a reference model $\pi_{ref}$ (which uses standard dense causal attention). Since the underlying attention computation is structurally different, how is this KL divergence computed and does this difference lead to optimization instability? More detail or analysis on this would strengthen the paper.

Details on Rollout Thresholding: The paper states that each rollout $o_n$ is generated with a random threshold $p_n \sim U(0,1)$ or within $[0.94, 0.975]$. It is not entirely clear if $p_n$ is sampled once at the start of the sequence generation and kept constant throughout the decoding of rollout $n$, or if it is sampled dynamically at each decoding step. Clarifying this generation protocol would improve reproducibility.

strengths: The core idea of explicitly reinforcing token sparsity via reinforcement learning (GRPO) is highly intuitive and addresses a key limitation of training-free and SFT-based pruning methods, which often plateau at moderate budgets.

The formulation of the joint efficiency-performance reward, particularly the use of the group-level indicator $C$ to prevent policy collapse under zero-correct rollouts, is well-designed and effective.
Comprehensive evaluation across 13 diverse image and video benchmarks demonstrates robust performance, showing that the model can be pruned down to ~25% token budget with negligible accuracy loss.

The paper is very well-written, with clear explanations, illustrative figures, and thorough ablation studies (e.g., investigating different sparse attention mechanisms, group sizes, and token sparsity evolution across layers).
weaknesses: The training overhead is relatively high due to the sequential execution of rollouts for different budget thresholds $p$, as different budgets prevent straightforward batching.

The reward formulation relies heavily on a binary correctness metric ($r_{per}$), which limits the training dataset to tasks with easily evaluable ground-truth answers (e.g., short-answer VQA) and may not scale easily to more complex or open-ended multimodal generation tasks.

There is a lack of deep discussion on how the KL divergence penalty interacts with the sparse attention mechanism, given that a highly sparse policy model's token distribution will naturally deviate from the full-attention reference model.

strengths: Promising Idea: Leveraging RL (specifically GRPO) to directly optimize the efficiency-performance tradeoff of MLLMs is an elegant and sensible direction.
Strong Empirical Results: The reduction of token ratios to ~23% with virtually zero degradation in accuracy across 13 diverse benchmarks (both image and video) is highly impressive.
Solid Base Models: The evaluation is conducted on competitive, state-of-the-art open-source MLLMs (Qwen2-VL and Qwen2.5-VL series).
weaknesses: Lack of physical latency/throughput measurements: While the token ratio is reduced to ~23%, actual wall-clock speedups (prefill time, decoding throughput, peak memory) are not presented. It is critical to show that this token sparsity translates to real-world performance gains on GPUs, especially since dynamic sparse attention patterns can be challenging to accelerate without custom GPU kernels.

Missing Ablation Studies: There are no ablations on key components. For example, it is unclear what happens if simple supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is used instead of RL, or how the reward weight coefficient between performance and efficiency affects the tradeoff curve.

Incomplete Technical and Training Details: The training details are very brief. It mentions using Video-R1-260k, but does not specify the number of samples used, the number of training steps, the learning rate, the number of groups N in GRPO, or the training compute requirements.

Lack of Analysis on Attention Maps: The paper claims that the token ratio decreases from ~80% to ~23% at the same threshold p=0.975. This implies the attention maps have become significantly sharper (entropy has decreased). Providing qualitative visualizations of attention maps or quantitative entropy analysis before and after ZipR1 would greatly strengthen the paper and validate this mechanism.
Short Paper Length and Overall Completeness: At only 4 pages of main content, the paper feels incomplete and lacks the depth, thoroughness, and analysis expected of a top-tier conference publication.

strengths: Novel and highly practical idea: Leveraging reinforcement learning (specifically GRPO) to post-train MLLMs for token sparsity is a creative approach that avoids the high cost of training from scratch.

Strong empirical results: Reducing the token ratio of Qwen2/2.5-VL models from ~80% down to ~23% while maintaining almost identical accuracy across 13 diverse image and video benchmarks is a highly impressive result.
Clear exposition: The paper is well-organized, with a clear explanation of ZipVL, the GRPO framework, and the reward formulation.
weaknesses: Severe lack of ablation studies and in-depth analysis: At only 4 pages of main content, the paper is missing crucial analyses. There are no trade-off curves showing performance vs. token ratio under varying inference thresholds $p$. There are also no ablation studies on the reward weights (the balance between $r_{per}$ and $r_{eff}$) or training curves showing how token ratio and accuracy evolve during RL training.

Missing training and implementation details: Essential details of the RL training process are omitted, such as the GRPO group size $N$, learning rate, batch size, and the number of training steps. Additionally, the paper does not explain how the binary correctness reward $r_{per}$ is evaluated for free-form or open-ended questions in the training dataset.

No physical efficiency/hardware metrics: While the token reduction ratio is a useful theoretical proxy, actual wall-clock speedups (latency in milliseconds) and memory savings (VRAM in GB) are not reported. Sparse attention mechanisms can introduce kernel overheads, so real hardware measurements are necessary to prove practical utility.

Unclear mechanism of policy-threshold interaction: During training, thresholds are sampled randomly ($p_n \sim U(0,1)$). It is not clearly explained how the model parameters $	heta$ adapt to these external thresholds. Does the model learn to naturally concentrate its attention scores on fewer tokens so that the Top-p threshold selects fewer elements? Some visualization of the learned attention maps compared to the reference model would greatly clarify this.

strengths: The idea of using Reinforcement Learning (specifically GRPO) to optimize the performance-efficiency trade-off under sparse attention is intuitive and interesting.
The evaluation spans a diverse set of 13 image and video benchmarks, showing promising token reduction numbers while maintaining baseline performance.
weaknesses: The manuscript is extremely short (only 4 pages of main text) and lacks the depth, analysis, and completeness expected for a top-tier AI conference.

Crucial implementation and training details are missing, such as which parameters are optimized (full tuning vs. LoRA), the hyperparameters for GRPO (learning rate, group size $N$, KL weight $\beta$), and the details of the training process (number of steps, epoch, computational cost).

The core mechanism behind the token ratio reduction is left unexplained. The paper sets the cumulative attention threshold $p = 0.975$ for both ZipVL and ZipR1, yet the token ratio drops drastically from ~80% to ~23%. The paper should analyze and visualize this phenomenon (e.g., via attention map visualizations or attention entropy analysis) to show if the policy network learns to produce sharper attention distributions.

There is a complete lack of ablation studies. The paper should present trade-off curves (performance vs. token ratio) across various threshold values of $p$, and analyze the impact of different reward weightings or the KL penalty coefficient.
The novelty is limited as the work is a straightforward combination of an existing sparse attention method (ZipVL) and a standard RL framework (GRPO).
